name: Pharmacogenomics
title: Pharmacogenomics
answer: Pharmacogenomics is the study of how inherited genetic variation changes a person's response to drugs, including metabolism, transport, and target binding. Within genomic medicine and precision therapeutics, it turns a patient's genotype into dosing and drug selection guidance. The AI Physician section covers models that combine pharmacogene results with clinical data to support prescribing. The scope includes germline variants in genes such as CYP2D6, CYP2C19, and SLCO1B1, as well as somatic tumor markers that affect oncology drugs. It also covers the clinical decision support systems that deliver these recommendations at the point of care.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Pharmacogenomics is the study of how inherited genetic variation changes a person's response to drugs, including metabolism, transport, and target binding. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Pharmacogenomic AI runs on curated knowledge bases such as PharmGKB and CPIC, which link gene variants to drug guidelines, along with variant call files from sequencing or genotyping arrays. Models are typically deployed as web services or embedded modules inside electronic health record systems, where they receive structured genotype and medication data. Storage and compute must meet health data protection requirements because raw genetic data are sensitive. Many implementations use cloud infrastructure with encryption and access controls, while some hospitals keep data on local servers. The main computational load is not heavy compared with imaging models, but it requires reliable integration with laboratory and pharmacy systems.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with translating raw genetic variants into star alleles and predicted phenotypes such as poor, intermediate, normal, or ultrarapid metabolizer. Rule-based systems then map these phenotypes to drug specific recommendations using guidelines from CPIC and other consortia. Machine learning models add a statistical layer, trained on genotype and phenotype cohorts to predict drug exposure, response, or adverse events when guidelines are incomplete. Natural language processing is used to extract drug gene evidence from published literature and clinical notes. Validation is done against measured drug levels, clinical outcomes, or prospectively collected pharmacogenomic data.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Pharmacogenomic data are genetic data, so consent, secondary use, and return of results are governed by stricter rules than ordinary clinical data. Models that recommend doses or drug choices can cause harm if a predicted phenotype is wrong, and the site tracks six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, a reminder that clinical decision support carries legal risk. Training data provenance matters because allele frequencies differ across populations, and a model trained mainly on one ancestry group may misclassify patients from another. Compliance pages on the site cover device regulation, data protection, and clinical decision support rules that apply to these tools. Institutions usually require that pharmacogenomic results be confirmed by a certified laboratory before they are acted on.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Pharmacogenomics is moving toward preemptive panel testing, where a patient's key pharmacogenes are sequenced once and stored for future prescribing decisions. Models are being developed to update recommendations automatically as new drug gene evidence appears, reducing the need for manual guideline review. Federated learning may allow training across hospital biobanks without moving raw genetic data, which would improve representation of diverse populations. The field is expanding beyond a small set of liver enzymes to include drug transporters, immune genes, and polygenic scores that capture many small effects. Over time, pharmacogenomic models are likely to merge with general medication safety AI, so that a single system flags both genetic and non genetic causes of adverse drug reactions.
